confirmedApply.title: ResolveMemo's eventsCache invalidates on trust()/untrust(), not just observe()/unobserve() as documented — false invariant in a doc comment, verified live
confirmedApply.detail:
The `ResolveMemo.eventsCache` doc comment (lines 440-450) asserts: "`applyStoreDelta` always produces a fresh `admit`/`observedById` object per `observe`/`unobserve` delta (never mutated in place), so identity comparison is exactly 'has anything been observed or unobserved since this array was built.'" This is false: `admit.ts`'s `applyDelta` (its `fromState`/`toState` helpers, admit.ts:348-370) unconditionally deep-clones `observedById` into a brand-new `Map`/`Record` on EVERY delta kind, including `trust`/`untrust`, which never touch `observedById`'s content at all. I verified this directly: `applyStoreDelta(EMPTY_STORE_STATE, {kind:'trust', pubkeys:['pk-x']}).admit.observedById === EMPTY_STORE_STATE.admit.observedById` evaluates to `false` (reference changes despite zero content change).

Consequence in `resolveRootMemoized` (store.ts:467-495): the per-root `memo.entries` cache (keyed on `chainEpoch`) correctly and cheaply short-circuits for any root already warm in the memo, since `chainEpoch` is untouched by trust/untrust (this path is what the existing SG2 test at store-property.test.ts:121-135 actually exercises — it only re-queries roots already warm in `memo.entries`, so it never reaches the `eventsCache` code path and does not catch this). But for any root resolved for the *first time* after an intervening `trust()`/`untrust()` call (a fresh memo, a new root, or simply the first `resolveRootBound` call following a trust change), the `memo.eventsCache?.observedById !== state.admit.observedById` check (store.ts:485) will spuriously fail even though the observed-event set is byte-identical, forcing a full unnecessary `Object.values(state.admit.observedById).filter(...)` materialization (store.ts:489) over the entire observed set — exactly the O(R × N) cost the memo's own doc comment says it exists to avoid, reintroduced specifically around trust changes.

This is not a wrong-output bug (resolve() still receives a content-identical events array), but it is a real, demonstrable, and previously-undocumented performance cliff triggered on the trust-mutation path this module explicitly optimizes for (D24's third epoch exists precisely so a `trustEpoch` bump stays cheap). Fix: gate the `eventsCache` rebuild on `state.observedEpoch` (which, per its own documented contract at store.ts:92/165, bumps only on `observe()`/`unobserve()` and never on `trust()`/`untrust()`) instead of `observedById` reference identity — a one-line, behavior-preserving change (same resolve() results, cheaper amortization) that doesn't touch any public surface or protocol semantics.
voteReasons:
Not refuted. I refute-tested this from five angles and the finding survives on substance.

1) FACTUAL VERIFICATION (failed to refute — verified live). I wrote and ran a scratch vitest probe (since deleted): (a) `applyStoreDelta(EMPTY_STORE_STATE, {kind:'trust',pubkeys:['pk-x']}).admit.observedById !== EMPTY_STORE_STATE.admit.observedById` — fresh reference, zero content change (observedEpoch stays 0, trustEpoch→1); same for untrust. Root cause confirmed in admit.ts:380: `applyDelta` unconditionally calls `fromState` (deep-clones observedById into a new Map, admit.ts:348-357) and `toState` (new Record via Object.fromEntries, admit.ts:361-370) on EVERY delta kind, and the `newly` guard in the trust branch only guards content, not reference. (b) After priming `memo.eventsCache`, applying trust, then resolving a not-yet-cached root: `memo.eventsCache` is rebuilt despite an identical observed set (store.ts:486-494), while warm roots short-circuit via `memo.entries`/chainEpoch (store.ts:484) — exactly as the finding describes. A sibling verifier independently wrote an equivalent probe with a real observed root and reached the same result.

2) NOT A DELIBERATE DOCUMENTED DECISION. docs/DECISIONS-2026-07-27.md records related tradeoffs (D24, D28, C3, C5, C10) but contains zero mention of eventsCache or this trust-path rebuild. VALIDATION-WIRING.md §4 calls the reference check 'correct' — but only for the correctness of the invalidIds gate (which genuinely still holds: invalidIds only changes inside an observe delta, which always produces a fresh observedById). No doc acknowledges the spurious trust-path cost.

3) THE TEST-GAP CLAIM IS ALSO CONFIRMED. The SG2 property test 'the Resolution memo is never invalidated by a trust-only delta' (store-property.test.ts:121-135) re-resolves only roots already warm in memo.entries, so it never reaches the eventsCache check — its name overclaims what it covers.

4) THE PROPOSED FIX IS SOUND AND VIOLATES NO INVARIANT. Gating on observedEpoch covers every content change of both observedById and invalidIds (both only change inside observe/unobserve deltas, which bump observedEpoch; trust/untrust never bump it — applyStoreDelta store.ts:407-423). Outputs of resolve() are unchanged; eventsCache is an internal opaque interface; no new epoch, no crypto, no exports change. The finding actually understates the doc-comment falsehood: no-op observe/unobserve deltas also produce a fresh observedById (unconditional bump at store.ts:347/401), where both gates behave identically — so the epoch gate is strictly no worse, and strictly better on trust/untrust.

5) SEVERITY IS OVERSTATED BUT THE FINDING IS NOT FRAMED AS A BUG. The 'exactly the O(R×N) cost' phrasing is hyperbole: after ONE rebuild the remaining R−1 roots share the rebuilt array, so the real extra cost is at most one O(N) materialization per trust delta followed by a cold-miss resolve (zero cost for warm roots). But the finding's core claim — 'a false invariant in a doc comment, verified live... not a wrong-output bug' — is exactly what it is: a verified-false doc comment plus a real, mild, one-per-trust-delta performance regression on the path D24's trustEpoch exists to keep cheap. The caveat narrows the impact, it does not refute the finding.

confirmedFlag.title: compareVersionTags loses precision on version fields wider than 2^53, silently reintroducing a digit-count ceiling
confirmedFlag.detail: parseVersionTag (line 194) does `Number(major)`/`Number(minor)`/`Number(patch)`, and compareVersionTags (line 211) subtracts those Numbers. The module's own doc comment for compareVersionTags advertises 'no fixed width and no digit-count ceiling in any field' as the entire point of the v0.7.0 amendment (F14), which retired the three-digit form specifically because it forced artificial limits (D45). But `Number()` silently loses integer precision beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 - 1, ~16 decimal digits). Verified: `Number('9007199254740993') === Number('9007199254740992')` (both round to 9007199254740992), so `compareVersionTags('scrutiny-v9007199254740993.0.0', 'scrutiny-v9007199254740992.0.0')` returns 0 (equal) even though the two tags are textually and numerically distinct — and more subtly, two adjacent large-but-distinct values in the range above 2^53 can compare in the wrong order after rounding. This is the same class of defect F14 was written to eliminate, just moved from a fixed digit count to an IEEE-754 mantissa width. It matters because compareVersionTags feeds VER-3's implementation-vs-declared-version check in validate.ts (`compareVersionTags(single, VERSION_TAG) > 0`), so a crafted event with an oversized version field could be miscompared relative to this implementation's own version. Fix would be to parse fields as BigInt (or reject/clamp fields exceeding a documented safe width) rather than Number, and to update the doc comment's 'no digit-count ceiling' claim to match whatever is actually guaranteed.

confirmedFlag.title: checkBinding's BD-3/4/5 endpoint typing and checkPatch's new PT-10/11 typing are coincidentally similar, not a real duplicate — leave them separate
confirmedFlag.detail:
Verdict: coincidental similarity, not worth extracting into a shared helper. Both functions share the shape "look up a referenced event, read its type, compare against an expectation, push issues on mismatch" — but every other dimension differs enough that a shared helper would need more configuration surface than the ~6 lines of duplication it would save, which is the textbook shallow-abstraction trade.

Concrete differences, read from the actual code:

1. Arity. checkBinding (lines 284-322) drives a `for` loop over a 2-element `endpoints` table (`root`/`link`), because it genuinely has two structurally identical roles. checkPatch (lines 374-395) has exactly one endpoint (`e root`) — there is no second role to justify the table/loop machinery, and adding it for a single call site would be the 'over-general abstraction used exactly once' smell this audit is explicitly watching for.

2. The type predicate shape differs, not just its value. checkBinding compares for exact equality against one `required` type per role (`observedType !== required`, root wants exactly 'product', link wants exactly 'metadata' — two different single-value comparisons carried in the `endpoints` table's `required` field). checkPatch checks set membership against two acceptable types in one branch (`rootType !== 'product' && rootType !== 'metadata'`) because a Patch's root may legitimately be *either* a Product or a Metadata. A shared predicate parameter would have to accept either a single value or a set, which is exactly the kind of parameter-shape branching that signals the two call sites don't actually want the same helper.

3. The issue-list shape per mismatch differs. A Binding typing violation always emits three issues with a role-dependent rule id: the per-role rule (`BD-3` or `BD-4`), plus the fixed `BD-5`, plus a `BD-7` *warning* for permanent caching (lines 299-309). A Patch typing violation emits exactly two issues, both fixed ids, both `error`, no warning-severity caching rule at all — deliberately, per the comment at lines 391-393 and SPEC-FEEDBACK-v0.6.0.md's F13 entry: PT-11's caching is already implied by UR-3, so no BD-7 analogue exists for Patch. A shared helper would need a variable-length, variable-severity issue list threaded in by the caller, which just re-externalizes the difference rather than hiding it.

4. checkBinding's loop interleaves an unrelated advisory check (BD-12's author-hint mismatch, lines 313-321) inside the same iteration as the typing check, with no analogue anywhere in checkPatch. Any shared helper would either have to also parameterize over this optional side-check or be called from checkBinding in addition to a separate BD-12 pass — either way it stops being 'the shared typing-check helper' and becomes a Binding-specific loop body that Patch doesn't want.

5. Control flow after a mismatch differs: checkBinding's loop uses `continue` (pending) or falls through to check BD-12 even after a typing mismatch, because both endpoints must still be visited independently; checkPatch has a single endpoint so it just falls through to the PT-7 lineage check below (lines 397-418), unconditionally, mismatch or not — there's no second endpoint to visit.

Given that, extracting a shared 'resolve and type-check one endpoint' helper would need parameters for: single-value-vs-set predicate, a caller-supplied issue list (varying in length and severity), and an optional side-check — at which point the helper is a thin pass-through with no real behavior of its own, and the two call sites remain exactly as easy to misread as if they were separate. This is exactly the kind of similarity worth documenting and leaving alone rather than 'fixing.' confirmedFlag.title: Trusted-but-mistyped Bindings still credit admission to their wrongly-typed endpoints (BD-3/BD-4/BD-5 gap)
confirmedFlag.detail: admit.ts's own top-of-file comment (lines 78-83) claims: "A malformed Binding (zero or several root/link markers, or an endpoint typed wrong) is already a BD-2/BD-10/BD-5 validity concern enforced by validate.ts before an event would ever reach this module in a real pipeline; admit does not re-derive that rejection." This is false for the actual pipeline. `bindingEndpoints()` (admit.ts:95-103) only checks that a Binding carries exactly one `e root` and one `e link` marker — it never checks that the referenced root id is actually a Product or the linked id actually a Metadata (BD-3/BD-4, surfaced as BD-5 by validate.ts's `checkBinding`, which is `error` severity: `issue('BD-5', 'error', 'Binding endpoints violate the typing rule; not admitted')`). `computeAdmission`'s Binding loop (admit.ts:198-205) and the incremental `bindingIsLive`/`activateBinding` path (admit.ts:388-399) both credit `binding:<id>` to both endpoints based only on marker-count success, trust in the Binding's own pubkey, and the Binding not being retracted -- never on validity. Meanwhile `store.ts` (packages/core/src/store.ts:318) folds every observed event into `admit`'s delta via `applyAdmitDelta` unconditionally, before and independent of computing that batch's `invalidIds` (the validity verdict is only computed afterward, in the per-event loop starting at line 326). So a Binding whose `e root` actually points at a Metadata and `e link` at a Product -- correctly flagged `invalidIds`-invalid via BD-7/BD-5 -- still credits `binding:<id>` to those two wrongly-typed endpoints in `AdmissionIndex`, and a trusted view would render them as admitted purely on the strength of an invalid Binding. `computeAdmission` (the oracle) has the identical gap, so oracle/incremental agreement (D29's cross-check) cannot catch this -- both paths share the same wrong answer. This exact gap is already documented as an open, unresolved design item in docs/VALIDATION-WIRING.md section 8 ("Design correction: a related but out-of-scope gap in admit.ts") and section 9's open question 1 ("needs its own decision before it is fixed"), written during a prior phase's design work -- but it is not listed in docs/AUDIT-2026-07-31.md nor in the current docs/QUALITY-AUDIT-2026-08-08.md findings log, so this audit round has not yet tracked it. `test/store.test.ts`'s existing BD-7 tests (`describe('BD-7 — permanent rejection once both endpoints contradict BD-3/BD-4')`) do not catch it either, because those tests never call `store.trust(...)`, so the malformed Binding never gets `direct-trust` and the credit path is never exercised -- the bug is real but currently untested in either direction. Fix requires a real decision (VALIDATION-WIRING.md §9 sketches two options: add a validity-verdict parameter to `computeAdmission`/`applyDelta`, or have `store.ts` pre-filter `bindingEvents` by validity before folding into admit's delta), which is exactly why this is being flagged rather than silently patched.

confirmedFlag.title: In-memory storage's deletion-hiding cache is invalidated by every put(), forcing a full O(total-events) rescan on the next query() even for puts unrelated to any deletion
confirmedFlag.detail:
`createInMemoryEventStorage`'s `put()` (store.ts:721-729) unconditionally sets `deletedCache = undefined` on every call, regardless of whether the batch contains a kind-5 event or an event that is the target of an already-observed kind-5. The next `query()` call with `includeDeleted` unset (the common case) then rebuilds `deletedCache` via `honouredlyDeletedIds(byId)` (store.ts:606-619, called at store.ts:732-733), which walks *every* stored event to find kind-5s and re-derive their honoured targets — an O(N) pass over the whole store, independent of how small the just-put batch was.

Phase 21's own stated goal (the doc comment at store.ts:621-635) was to replace 'one Map plus a full scan per filter' with real per-key indexes so that `query()` doesn't pay O(N) per call. For any workload that interleaves writes and reads (a relay-shaped consumer: ingest an event, then immediately serve subscribers), this deletion cache becomes the dominant cost on the very next `query()` after *every* `put()`, effectively re-imposing the O(N) scan the indexing work was meant to eliminate — the kind/tag/e-tag indexes prune candidates for the *predicate*, but the deletion-visibility filter still pays full price every time a write has occurred since the last read, whether or not that write had anything to do with deletion.

A cheaper, still-correct alternative exists without changing behavior: only invalidate/incrementally update `deletedCache` when the put batch contains a kind-5 event, or contains an event whose id is already a target of some observed kind-5 (i.e., only DEL-relevant arrivals need to touch the cache) — normal Product/Metadata/Binding/Patch traffic, which is the overwhelming majority of writes, would leave the cache untouched. I'm flagging this for a human rather than proposing the change directly because getting the incremental-invalidation condition exactly right (DEL-1 pubkey match, DEL-6 kind-5-can't-be-deleted, DEL-8 target-not-yet-observed) without silently under-invalidating (which *would* be a real correctness bug, not just a perf one) needs its own test coverage before landing, not a mechanical edit.

Every factual claim in the finding verifies against the code. put() (store.ts:721-729) sets `deletedCache = undefined` unconditionally for every event, with no DEL-relevance check; query() (store.ts:732-733) rebuilds it via honouredlyDeletedIds (store.ts:606-619), which iterates `byId.values()` — a literal O(total-stored-events) pass — regardless of batch size or whether the writes had anything to do with deletion. Phase 21's stated purpose (IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN.md §Phase 21; code comment store.ts:621-635) was to replace 'one Map plus a full scan per filter' with real indexes precisely so query() stops paying O(N) per call; the deletion-visibility layer is a documented exception to that win for any interleaved write/read workload.

Refutation attempts, all failed:
(1) Factually wrong? No — line-by-line verification confirms the unconditional invalidation and the full-byId scan.
(2) Deliberate documented decision? No. The inline comment ('invalidated on put (any arrival can add a kind 5 or a target)') describes the behavior and its conservative rationale but records no weighing or rejection of the finer condition; docs/DECISIONS-2026-07-27.md (append-only) has no entry for this tradeoff, and neither QUALITY-AUDIT-2026-08-08.md nor AUDIT-2026-07-31.md §5 addresses invalidation granularity (AUDIT-2026-07-31.md §5 item 3 only complains the deletion scan was *uncached*, which Phase 21 fixed — it does not bless blanket invalidation).
(3) Proposed fix violates a hard invariant? No — it's a pure store-internal change (no crypto, no exports change, no dynamic import). The reviewer's own correctness caution (DEL-1 pubkey match, DEL-6 kind-5-not-deletable, DEL-8 target-arriving-after-deletion) is sound review hygiene, not a defect in the finding: the completeness condition 'invalidate only if the batch contains a kind-5 OR an event whose id is already an honoured target of an observed kind-5' is checkable cheaply via the existing eTagIdx/kindIdx per arrival, and Nostr id immutability means put-replacement can't change DEL relevance.
(4) Severity overstated? Only mildly in constant-factor terms — the rescan is a cheap kind-check per event rather than a full matchesFilter predicate pass — but the finding's asymptotic core is accurate and honestly scoped ('for any workload that interleaves writes and reads').

Notably, the situation is, if anything, slightly worse than the finding states in a way that supports it: honouredlyDeletedIds doesn't even use the kindIdx index Phase 21 built (iterating `byId` instead of `kindIdx.get(5)`), so a zero-correctness-risk improvement exists alongside the reviewer's riskier incremental-invalidation option. The finding survives scrutiny.

All factual claims verified against the code: put() invalidates deletedCache per event unconditionally (store.ts:727), and the next query() without includeDeleted rebuilds it via honouredlyDeletedIds, a full O(N) walk over every stored event resolving kind-5 e-tag targets (store.ts:606-619, 732-734), regardless of batch relevance. No refuting evidence found: the tradeoff is not recorded in docs/DECISIONS-2026-07-27.md (STORE.md §7's 'no deletion-specific cache' concerns resolve.ts, not this adapter), the code comment at store.ts:633-634 documents the rule but its rationale ('any arrival can add a kind 5 or a target') supports conservative correctness without precluding the conditional-invalidation refinement, and a test asserting the invalidation behavior exists, showing intent but not foreclosing improvement. But the load-bearing claim — unconditional per-put invalidation re-imposes a full O(total-events) rescan on the next read, and a safe, invariant-compliant scoping existed — is verified in code and was never reasoned through in the project's own decision record. Existing tests (storage-indexes.test.ts:272) assert the invalidation happens (correctness), not that the tradeoff was chosen. The finding stands.

confirmedFlag.title: Record-key prototype hazard: an event id of "__proto__" silently corrupts AdmissionIndex/AdmitState and diverges the incremental path from the oracle
confirmedFlag.detail: toState (admit.ts:361-371) builds its plain-object views with plain assignment: `reasons[id] = [...]` and `liveBindings[id] = endpoints`; computeAdmission's oracle does the same at `out[id] = ...` (~admit.ts:214). JS semantics (verified): `o['__proto__'] = x` sets the object's prototype instead of an own property — the key vanishes from Object.keys/Object.entries, yet a property lookup still returns the inherited value. Verified end-to-end consequences: (a) immediately after the delta, `isAdmitted(toIndex(state), '__proto__')` returns TRUE because it reads the inherited array's length; (b) on the NEXT applyDelta, fromState iterates Object.entries — own keys only — so the '__proto__' event's direct-trust reason AND its liveBindings entry are silently dropped, while observedById (built via Object.fromEntries, which is __proto__-safe) keeps the event observed. resyncBinding then sees a still-observed Binding with no direct-trust and no liveBindings entry forever — the incremental state now disagrees with computeAdmission's oracle (which says the binding is trusted → live → endpoints admitted). Reachability is real: nothing in validate.ts or store.ts checks id format (grepped — no eventIdMatches/hex check anywhere before admission; ids come straight from relay-supplied JSON), so a hostile event with id "__proto__" passes V-validation and lands here. Doubly dangerous: the AG1 property gate cannot catch it because BOTH sides (toState and computeAdmission's out) use the same vulnerable representation, so they fail identically and compare equal. Fix direction: build these records with Object.fromEntries (or null-prototype objects) in both toState and computeAdmission, and/or make isAdmitted use Object.hasOwn; also worth a property-generator id that occasionally emits '__proto__'/'constructor' so the gate actually sees the shape.

CONFIRMED empirically (temporary vitest repro against packages/core/src/admit.ts, deleted after run):
1. Representation: toState (admit.ts:361-371) builds `reasons`/`liveBindings` as plain `{}` records via plain assignment (`reasons[id] = [...]`, `liveBindings[id] = endpoints`); computeAdmission's oracle does the same (`out[id] = [...]`, admit.ts:215-216). 2. Immediately post-delta: `isAdmitted(toIndex(state), '__proto__')` returns TRUE via the inherited prototype array while `Object.keys` shows nothing (own keys: []). Since AdmitState is plain data meant for serialization, a JSON round-trip would silently lose the entry.
3. Next-delta corruption: fromState's Object.entries drops the '__proto__' direct-trust reason and its liveBindings entry; the event survives in observedById. After that, the incremental path reports the binding itself NOT admitted while the oracle still reports it admitted (isAdmitted: false vs true) — a real incremental-vs-oracle divergence.
4. Decisive divergence the finding didn't even name: the dropped liveBindings entry breaks the D23 side-table invariant, resurrecting the exact sticky-admission bug the module exists to prevent. The endpoints' `binding:__proto__` credit is carried over as an own key and can NEVER be removed (deactivateBinding's guard requires the wiped liveBindings entry). Verified: after `untrust(PK_OTHER)`, incremental still admits both endpoints (`reasons[root.id] = ['binding:__proto__']`) while the oracle correctly revokes them — a phantom admission surviving trust revocation, permanent and unrecoverable.
5. Reachability: applyDelta/computeAdmission/EMPTY_ADMIT_STATE/isAdmitted are all public barrel exports (index.ts:86-95); admit.ts's reducer is a documented direct-consumption API for relay-supplied events. validate.ts has no id-format check (confirmed by grep — the only id check, eventIdMatches, is a caller-injected helper unused inside the admission path).

DETAILS IN THE FINDING THAT ARE WRONG (noted, but they do not save the code):
(a) The stated endpoint-divergence direction is backwards. The finding claims the incremental path drops endpoint admission while the oracle keeps it; empirically the incremental path RETAINS stale endpoint credit and AGREES with the oracle until revocation — the real divergence is the binding's own lost admission plus post-revocation sticky credit (worse than described, not better).
(b) 'Nothing in store.ts checks id format' is inaccurate: createStore REQUIRES an injected `verify` covering 'signature AND id recompute (SIG-1)' (store.ts:502, no default, D18), so the blessed store.add() path rejects any non-hex id. Exposure is via the public applyDelta API used directly (a supported path) or the explicit documented trustUnverified/verified bypasses.
(c) 'Both sides fail identically so the AG1 gate cannot catch it' is only true for immediate snapshots; after further deltas the own-key sets diverge and the raw toEqual comparison DOES flag it (verified). The compound AG1 gate's actual blindness is that its generators only emit 64-hex ids — which the finding itself half-acknowledges by recommending generator coverage.

Verdict: The load-bearing thesis — a record-key prototype hazard at the cited location that silently corrupts AdmissionIndex/AdmitState and makes the incremental path diverge from the oracle — is factually correct and empirically reproduced, including a permanent phantom-admission-after-revocation state that violates the module's own D23 guarantee. The proposed fix direction (Object.fromEntries/null-prototype records in toState and computeAdmission, Object.hasOwn in isAdmitted, 'proto-hostile ids in the property generators) is sound and violates none of the project's hard invariants. Survives, with severity arguably understated rather than overstated.

refuted.title: T1's uniqueness count ignores the oldNoEol marker, causing a spurious ambiguous-match halt where the module's own design doc says the marker should disambiguate
refuted.detail:
`occurrences(lines, hunk.oldPat)` at line 311 counts every textual occurrence of the pattern with no regard to `hunk.oldNoEol`; the EOF-consistency check (`spliceAt`'s case-A/B branches in patch-matcher.ts:174-201) only runs afterward, against whichever single match T1 already picked. If the same pattern occurs twice — once at the true end of content (consistent with `oldNoEol`) and once mid-file (inconsistent with it) — `occurrences` reports `count === 2` and the hunk HALTs as `ambiguous-match` before the EOF marker is ever consulted, even though only one of the two textual matches is actually a valid position for this hunk.

Confirmed by executing the untracked `packages/core/test/zz-verify-bug.test.ts` already present in this working tree (again, I only ran it, made no edits): content `'x
DUP1
DUP2
y
DUP1
DUP2'` (no trailing newline) with a hunk whose old side is `DUP1
DUP2` marked `\ No newline at end of file` halts with `ambiguous-match`, even though the mid-file occurrence (at line 2) cannot possibly be what the hunk means — it isn't the end of the file, and the hunk explicitly asserts it is.

This directly contradicts `docs/PATCH-MATCHER.md` §4's own framing: "`oldNoEol` is additionally part of the match predicate: a 'no newline at EOF' hunk whose pattern occurs only mid-file has no valid position, and case A rejects it rather than relocating" — that sentence describes filtering candidates by EOF-consistency, but the code only ever validates the single candidate T1's plain-text count already settled on. Whether the correct fix is to filter candidate positions by EOF-consistency before counting (so the case above applies cleanly) or whether a strict textual reading of T1 ('the pattern MUST occur exactly once') really does mandate treating this as ambiguous regardless of EOF markers, is a judgment call — the spec doesn't address this composition explicitly, so it may warrant a SPEC-FEEDBACK entry (like F6/F12 elsewhere in this same file) rather than a silent behavior change. No regression case in patch-regressions.ts currently pins either reading.
voteReasons:
Attempted every refutation angle; the finding's factual core is verified, not misattributed, and not a recorded decision.

1. CODE BEHAVIOR — CONFIRMED BY EXECUTION. I ran the untracked packages/core/test/zz-verify-bug.test.ts myself (no edits): content 'x\nDUP1\nDUP2\ny\nDUP1\nDUP2' (no trailing newline) with old side 'DUP1\nDUP2' marked '\ No newline at end of file' halts with status 'halt' / reason 'ambiguous-match' / rule T1, detail 'matches the current content in 2 places (first at lines 2 and 5)'. The mid-file occurrence at line 2 cannot satisfy the old-side EOF assertion, so only one of the two textual matches is a semantically valid position — yet the hunk halts before the EOF marker is consulted. Control case (single occurrence at EOF) applies correctly. Code reading confirms the mechanism: patch.ts:311 calls occurrences(lines, hunk.oldPat) — a purely textual scan in patch-matcher.ts — and halts on count>1; spliceAt's case-A/B EOF-consistency checks (patch-matcher.ts ~174-201) run only afterward against the single index T1 already chose.

2. DOC CONTRADICTION — REAL, with one caveat. docs/PATCH-MATCHER.md §1 formally defines candidate positions as 'every i ∈ [0, |L|−k] such that L[i..i+k) === oldPat element-wise, and the EOF constraint of §4 holds at i', and §2 ('How T1 uniqueness is proven') says to count 'all candidates' over the whole content with ≥2 → ambiguous. Under the doc's own definition, the finding's scenario has exactly one candidate → apply. The code counts textual occurrences instead. Caveat: the sentence the finding quotes from §4 ('case A rejects it rather than relocating') actually describes post-hoc rejection — the code's mechanism — for the single-occurrence case, so the doc is internally tensioned (§1+§2 filter; §4 validates after the fact) and the finding's quote selection is slightly weak. This is a misattribution of emphasis, not a refutation: §1+§2 unambiguously match the finding's 'match predicate' framing, and the doc-code divergence exists whichever section you privilege.

3. NOT A DELIBERATE RECORDED DECISION. DECISIONS-2026-07-27.md contains nothing on the T1-uniqueness × EOF-marker composition (only unrelated mentions). SPEC-FEEDBACK-v0.6.0.md F1–F14 were scanned: F6 is the T2/T3 shift, F12 is the RL-2 unit, F13/F14 are validity/tag gaps — none records this tradeoff. patch-regressions.ts pins only unmarked ambiguous-match cases (t1/ambiguous-relocation, t1/adjacent-duplicate, t3 case) and single-occurrence EOF cases (the eof-mismatch case at line 168 has pattern '-b' occurring once in 'a\nb\n'). No test or decision pins either reading of the composition.

4. NOT UNREACHABLE. makePatch with context 3 would rarely produce such a hunk, but P1's context obligation is a producer SHOULD only, T2 itself presumes zero-context hunks exist, C7/C8 oblige consumers to accept any grammatical payload, and CHN-3 applies the same rules to foreign/overlay patches — so adversarial or hand-authored payloads reach this path. A severity discount is fair (fail-closed halt, no content corruption, narrow trigger), but it is not zero.

5. SPEC IS SILENT — and the finding says so. Normative T1 (protocol-spec.md v0.6.1, line 560) defines the pattern as 'context lines together with its removed (-) lines' and halts on 2+ occurrences with no mention of EOF markers; a strict reading supports the code. The finding explicitly anticipates this and recommends the correct disposition: a SPEC-FEEDBACK entry (like F6/F12) rather than a silent behavior change. The spec-silence argument therefore does not refute the finding — it is part of the finding.

The surviving claim after adversarial review: the reference implementation halts a hunk that has exactly one semantically valid position, contradicting its own design document's candidate-enumeration definition, with the divergence unrecorded anywhere. Accurate, narrow, correctly framed as needing spec feedback rather than an unilateral fix. Does not survive → survives: refuted = false.

The empirical claim holds (I ran the tree's zz-verify-bug.test.ts unmodified: 'x
DUP1
DUP2
y
DUP1
DUP2' + oldNoEol hunk halts with ambiguous-match at patch.ts:319-324, before spliceAt's case-A check at patch-matcher.ts:174-184 ever runs). But the finding's framing as a correctness bug contradicting the module's own design doc does not hold.

(1) The doc's normative section for the count is PATCH-MATCHER.md §2, whose verdict table is unconditional: 'count all candidates over the whole of L' -> 0 halt, >=2 halt ambiguous-match, exactly 1 apply. oldNoEol appears nowhere in §2, and the code implements it exactly. (2) The quoted §4 sentence, read in context, is about a DIFFERENT case: §4 states the EOF rules are 'applied at the single proven match index', and the sentence describes a hunk whose pattern 'occurs ONLY mid-file has no valid position, and case A rejects it rather than relocating' — the single-occurrence case, which the code implements exactly (eof-mismatch halt via case A). It never says the marker narrows a multi-occurrence count to one candidate; 'part of the match predicate' is at most loose wording. (3) T1's normative rule text is unconditional (rules.ts:815: 'context+`-` lines MUST occur exactly once in current content'; spec §5.3 same), so pre-filtering candidates by the marker would reinterpret T1 — the finding's own detail concedes this 'may warrant a SPEC-FEEDBACK entry rather than a silent behavior change', which undercuts filing it as a code bug. (4) The halt is the designed fail-closed behavior per D30 (the T1/T2/T3 determinism gate exists precisely to refuse what git apply silently relocates), and the designed remedy already exists: build.ts's producer-side context-widening loop regenerates with wider context, which disambiguates this exact case (EOF occurrence is preceded by 'y', mid-file one by 'x'). No regression case pins either reading because the composition is genuinely spec-silent, but the current code matches both §2's explicit table and T1's unconditional rule text.

Verdict: refuted. The code contradicts neither §2 (which it implements verbatim) nor §4 (whose demonstrated single-candidate case it handles correctly), T1's rule text mandates the halt, and the severity is overstated — the outcome is a recoverable fail-closed halt with an existing producer-side mitigation, not a defect. At most this warrants a one-line wording clarification in PATCH-MATCHER.md §4, not a correctness fix.

The finding's narrow factual claim is true — I reproduced it: content 'x\nDUP1\nDUP2\ny\nDUP1\nDUP2' (no trailing newline) with an oldNoEol-marked hunk whose pattern is DUP1\nDUP2 halts as ambiguous-match (rule T1), because occurrences() at patch.ts:311 counts textual occurrences only and spliceAt()'s case-A EOF check (patch-matcher.ts:174-201) runs afterward, on a single proven match. But the finding's core assertion — that this is a correctness bug contradicting the module's own design doc — fails under scrutiny on three grounds.

1) The code implements the normative spec literally. The upstream protocol spec (~/scrutiny-fabric/docs/protocol-spec.md, §5.3, A-layer) defines T1 as: 'Each hunk's context lines together with its removed (-) lines MUST occur exactly once in the current content… If the pattern occurs two or more times, the patch is also invalid.' It grants no EOF-marker disambiguation. C5 says only that the `\` marker 'signals the absence of a trailing newline… consumers MUST handle it per the unified-diff spec' — unified-diff semantics make the marker newline-state information, not a candidate filter or uniqueness override. Under the normative text, a pattern occurring twice is invalid, full stop; the ambiguous-match halt is the spec-faithful result, and the finding's implied fix — filtering T1 candidates by oldNoEol-consistency and applying at the unique EOF-consistent position — is behavior the spec does not grant (its strict wording arguably forbids it).

2) The quoted design-doc sentence is misread. PATCH-MATCHER.md §4 frames the C5 rules explicitly as 'applied at the single proven match index'. The cited sentence describes 'a no-newline-at-EOF hunk whose pattern occurs ONLY mid-file' — i.e., the single-match case. That case is handled exactly as documented: the unique mid-file match reaches spliceAt's case A and halts as eof-mismatch 'rather than relocating'. The sentence validates one position; it does not describe filtering among multiple textual candidates, which is the reviewer's generalization, not the doc's claim. PATCH-MATCHER.md §2's own T1 table (count all candidates; >=2 → halt ambiguous) is what governs the multi-occurrence case, and the code matches it.

3) The implied fix would be worse, and the severity is overstated. T1's strictness exists (D30, PATCH-MATCHER §2) to guarantee cross-implementation determinism because git apply/jsdiff silently relocate. If some implementations filtered candidates by EOF-consistency and others counted textually, they would diverge on exactly this adversarial input — one applies, the other halts — recreating the non-determinism T1 was built to eliminate. The current behavior is fail-closed (a halt never produces wrong content; the control test confirms the unique-EOF case applies cleanly). No DECISIONS-2026-07-27.md entry records the composition, but none is needed: the behavior follows the normative rule text. At most, the spec's silence on T1∩C5 composition could justify a SPEC-FEEDBACK clarification entry — a documentation nicety, not a correctness defect at patch.ts:311. As a category-correctness finding asserting a bug and a doc contradiction, it is refuted.

refuted.title: pendingAwaiting leaks a stale entry when a Binding's two awaited endpoints resolve asymmetrically (one triggers 'invalid', the other's registration is never cleared)
refuted.detail:
store.ts's own comment at lines 264-265 claims: 'a still-unresolved awaited id from an earlier partial check is re-derived, not pruned, by the re-validation below.' This is false for a Binding awaiting BOTH endpoints (BD-6) when one endpoint's arrival makes the other endpoint's typing check produce a terminal 'invalid' verdict while the other endpoint is still unobserved.

Mechanism: validate.ts's checkBinding (lines 258-333) loops over BOTH endpoints unconditionally (`for (const { ref, role, required, rule } of endpoints)`, no early return), so it can simultaneously push an error issue for one endpoint (wrong type -> BD-3/BD-4 + BD-5 'error') AND push the other, still-unobserved endpoint's id onto `awaiting` in the same call. But validateEvent (lines 101-107) checks `hasError(issues)` BEFORE checking `awaiting.length`, so once any error is present it returns `{status: 'invalid', issues}` -- a variant that carries no `awaiting` field at all. The populated `awaiting` array is silently discarded.

Back in store.ts, `applyVerdict` (lines 157-169) only ever ADDS entries to `pendingAwaiting` when `verdict.status === 'pending'`; on an 'invalid' verdict it does nothing beyond `invalidIds.add(event.id)`. The caller loop that triggered the re-check (lines 260-281) only removes the ONE awaited-id entry that just arrived (`removeAwaiting(pendingAwaiting, event.id, pendingId)`), never any of the event's OTHER still-registered awaited-id entries.

Concrete repro: Binding B has `e root` -> X (unobserved) and `e link` -> L (unobserved). `add([B])`: verdict is pending, awaiting=[X, L]; pendingAwaiting[X]={B}, pendingAwaiting[L]={B}. Now `add([X])` where X turns out to be a Patch, not a Product (wrong type for the root role): processObservedEvent(X) finds pendingAwaiting[X]={B}, removes that one entry, then re-validates B. checkBinding now sees root=X (wrong type, pushes BD-3/BD-5 error) and continues to link=L (still unobserved, pushes L onto awaiting) -- but hasError wins, so validateEvent returns 'invalid' and the awaiting=[L] is thrown away. store correctly adds B to invalidIds, but pendingAwaiting[L]={B} is NEVER cleaned up. If L never arrives, this entry sits in `StoreState.pendingAwaiting` forever (unbounded growth for a long-running store). Even explicitly `unobserve([B])` doesn't clean it: the unobserve cleanup path (lines 370-375) only fires `if (verdict.status === 'pending')`, and re-validating the already-terminally-invalid B returns 'invalid', not 'pending', so the stale pendingAwaiting[L] entry survives B's own removal too.

This is a genuine, previously-unreported gap (not the same as the already-fixed P6/P5 items or the documented arrival-order-dependent chainEpoch quirk). It's also structurally invisible to the existing SG1 confluence gate: `toStoreView` (STORE.md §9) deliberately excludes `pendingAwaiting` from the compared projection (for legitimate, unrelated reasons -- arrival-order-dependent cache bookkeeping), so no existing property test can catch this leak even if the fuzzer happened to generate the triggering interleaving. All existing BD-7 tests in store.test.ts either deliver both endpoints in one batched add() call (never reaching the asymmetric partial-await case, since admitAfter.observedById already contains every batch member before checkBinding runs) or don't probe pendingAwaiting content after an asymmetric-arrival BD-7 rejection.

Suggested fix direction (for a human to design, not one-line): either (a) have checkBinding short-circuit and stop appending to `awaiting` once an error is pushed for an already-checked endpoint (mirroring checkPatch's own return-immediately-after-awaiting discipline at validate.ts:378-379/404-405), so `awaiting` and error issues are never populated together in the same verdict, or (b) have store.ts's applyVerdict, on a fresh 'invalid' verdict, proactively scrub the event's id out of every pendingAwaiting bucket it might still be registered under (requires either a reverse id->awaited-ids index or an accepted O(pendingAwaiting) scan).
voteReasons: The finding's code mechanism is factually real — I reproduced it empirically with a scratch vitest: Binding B added pending on both endpoints (pendingAwaiting = {X:[B], L:[B]}); when wrong-typed root X arrives, checkBinding pushes BD-3/BD-5 error AND pushes L onto awaiting, validateEvent's hasError-before-awaiting check discards awaiting, applyVerdict adds B to invalidIds and leaves pendingAwaiting = {L:[B]}; unobserve(B) does not remove it either (the unobserve cleanup only fires on a 'pending' verdict, and B is now terminally 'invalid'). But the finding is REFUTED on its central claims — 'genuine, previously-unreported gap' and 'leak': (1) docs/VALIDATION-WIRING.md §2 lines 144-147 explicitly documents this exact case under 'resolves to invalid' and classifies it as 'a bounded, self-cleaning cost, not a leak, since each event can arrive at most once' — the reviewer apparently never read the design doc that anticipated precisely this residual-registration scenario. (2) The doc's self-cleaning claim is empirically true: in my repro, when L eventually arrived, pendingAwaiting drained to {} — the residual entry is consumed even after B itself was unobserved (processObservedEvent hits the observedById[pendingId] === undefined continue path after removeAwaiting). (3) The only permanent-persistence case is the awaited id never arriving, which is indistinguishable at the protocol level from the already-accepted, by-design behavior of any pending event awaiting a never-arriving id — the buffer inherently retains such registrations with no signal to prune. (4) Zero correctness impact: invalidIds is exactly correct, all verdicts correct, and pendingAwaiting's exclusion from the SG1-compared StoreView is documented design (STORE.md §3/§9, VALIDATION-WIRING.md 281-284), not concealment. (5) Both suggested fix directions are worse: short-circuiting checkBinding would change validateEvent's observable issue output (dropping the second endpoint's BD-3/4/5 issue and BD-6 context from a verdict that consumers of validate.ts see), and invalid-time scrubbing requires a reverse index or O(pendingAwaiting) scan per invalid verdict — a heavier recurring cost than the documented bounded residual. The store.ts:264-265 comment the finding attacks is incomplete (it describes the still-pending branch; the invalid branch is covered by the design doc), at most a doc nit, not a correctness bug.

The finding's code-level mechanism is accurate (verified directly): checkBinding loops both endpoints without early return, validateEvent checks hasError before awaiting.length and discards a populated `awaiting` on an 'invalid' verdict, applyVerdict never scrubs pre-existing pendingAwaiting registrations on 'invalid', and the unobserve cleanup is gated on 'pending'. So pendingAwaiting[L]={B} genuinely survives when a Binding goes terminal-invalid on one endpoint while the other is unobserved.

However, the finding is refuted on decisiveness grounds:

1. NOT previously unreported — docs/VALIDATION-WIRING.md §2 explicitly anticipates this exact scenario in its 'resolves to invalid' draining outcome: 'If some other, still-unresolved awaited id was left registered for this pending id from an earlier partial check, it is harmlessly consumed (and immediately re-derives the same invalid verdict, idempotently) the one time that id itself eventually arrives — a bounded, self-cleaning cost, not a leak, since each event can arrive at most once.' This is a deliberate, reasoned, documented design decision, not an oversight — exactly the refutation ground the verification instructions name.

2. Severity overstated: 'unbounded growth' contradicts the documented bound. The dedup gate guarantees each event arrives at most once, so a stale entry fires at most one idempotent re-validation (re-deriving the same 'invalid' verdict — functionally inert — or short-circuiting on observedById[pendingId] === undefined after the event is removed). For a never-arriving awaited id the residual is one small id-map entry, never an incorrect verdict in any observable view.

3. The SG1 invisibility the finding flags is itself deliberate: pendingAwaiting is documented (STORE.md §3/§9, DECISIONS-2026-07-27.md) as excluded from the confluence-tested StoreView because its contents are 'legitimately arrival-order-dependent bookkeeping'.

4. The unobserve non-cleanup follows the project's established precedent: chainMembership is deliberately left 'stale-but-correct' on unobserve and overlayAwaiting is 'never mutated on unobserve, in either dimension' (DECISIONS C10). Retaining stale id-bookkeeping is the chosen house style, preferred over refcount/reverse-index complexity the finding's fix would require.

5. The store.ts:264-265 comment ('re-derived, not pruned') is terse for the terminal-invalid branch, but VALIDATION-WIRING.md §2 explicitly specifies that branch ('do not re-add any awaiting entry for it'), so the code matches its spec — a comment nitpick at most, not a correctness bug.

No hard invariant is at stake; no functional incorrectness is observable. Refuted as a documented, reasoned tradeoff with overstated severity.

The code-level mechanism is verified accurate (checkBinding loops both endpoints without early return; validateEvent checks hasError before awaiting.length and discards awaiting on invalid; applyVerdict never scrubs prior registrations on invalid; the wakeup loop removes only the arrived id's slot; unobserve cleanup fires only on a pending re-verdict; the store.ts:264-265 comment is imprecise about the invalid outcome). However, the finding's central claims of novelty and defect are refuted by docs/VALIDATION-WIRING.md §2 ('Draining, on a later arrival' -> 'resolves to invalid' bullet), which explicitly analyzes this exact scenario: 'If some other, still-unresolved awaited id was left registered for this pending id from an earlier partial check, it is harmlessly consumed (and immediately re-derives the same invalid verdict, idempotently) the one time that id itself eventually arrives — a bounded, self-cleaning cost, not a leak, since each event can arrive at most once.' This is a documented, reasoned design decision, not a previously-unreported gap. The decision is sound: invalid verdicts are monotone-permanent (BD-7/UR-3 — an observed endpoint's type cannot change), so the eventual-arrival re-validation is idempotent; removeAwaiting runs BEFORE the observedById check in the wakeup loop (store.ts:265-267), so the entry self-cleans on the awaited id's arrival even if the awaiter was itself unobserved (weakening the finding's permanence claim — 'if L never arrives' is the only stale case). No consumer-visible incorrectness results: pendingAwaiting feeds only the wakeup loop, and its exclusion from the confluence-tested StoreView is itself documented as deliberate arrival-order-dependent bookkeeping (VALIDATION-WIRING.md §4, STORE.md §9) — the 'SG1 invisibility' is by design. Severity is overstated: the worst case is memory dead-weight proportional to admitted invalid events with unresolved references, the identical growth class as the deliberately-monotone invalidIds and the 'stale-but-still-correct' chainMembership precedent. The suggested fixes are also defective: fix (a) (checkBinding short-circuit) cannot remove the actual leak source — the stale registration originates from the ORIGINAL pending verdict's addAwaiting, not from the discarded awaiting array of the invalid re-verdict — so (a) is cosmetic while degrading validate.ts's per-endpoint diagnostic completeness; fix (b) (reverse index or O(n) scan) spends exactly the machinery the documented decision weighed and rejected. At most this warrants a one-line comment clarification at store.ts:264-265 noting the invalid case leaves the slot for arrival-triggered self-cleaning per VALIDATION-WIRING.md §2, not a correctness fix.

refuted.title: cascade() is O(patches × depth): each fixpoint round rescans every candidate
refuted.detail: The `for (let changed = true; changed;)` loop re-scans all `candidates` once per propagation round, so a deleted first patch in a depth-D chain costs D rounds × N candidates = O(N·D). Realistic depth is ≤1 (AUDIT-2026-07-31 §4), but resolve() accepts an arbitrary observed set and no §5.4 ceiling bounds chain length — an adversarial corpus of ~10k chained patches turns deletion handling into ~10^8 set lookups per resolve call. A children-index BFS from the directly-deleted candidates (build parent→children map once, walk it) is O(N) and yields the identical set: the operator is monotone so the fixpoint is unique, and `removed` is only ever membership-tested, so no observable behavior changes. Same for the walk's existing children map — it could be shared with cascade instead of building the parent relation twice.
voteReasons:
The complexity claim is technically true in the worst case (naive fixpoint = O(N·D), N patches, D chain depth), but the finding does not hold up on four grounds:

1. THREAT PREMISE INFLATED. cascade() runs over `linkable`, which is `rootAuthored` — patches with pubkey === root.pubkey filtered through the PT-6/OV-8 link rule (resolve.ts:278-286). A foreign adversary cannot add chain links; the claimed "adversarial corpus of ~10k chained patches" requires the root author's own signing key. An attacker holding the root key can harm that product far more directly, so this is not a reachable DoS surface for the stated threat model.

2. SEVERITY / SCOPE. AUDIT-2026-07-31 §4 measured the real corpus at chain depth "0 or 1 — max 1" (line 206), and C3 of the same audit explicitly declined engineering for deeper corpora — D28's depth-driven LRU was judged over-engineered and never built. At D ≤ 1, O(N·D) = O(N) with a tiny constant (≤2 passes); the ≥3-round case never occurs in any in-scope input. The finding itself concedes this.

3. DELIBERATE, DOCUMENTED DESIGN. RESOLVE.md §2 specifies the algorithm as "Three filters, in this order, then a fixed point ... Computed as a fixed point over the parent→children relation, which is order-independent by construction", and its confluence table cites "the cascade is a fixed point" as the order-independence guarantee. The 12-line implementation transcribes the documented spec verbatim; that correspondence is a feature of a reference implementation, not an oversight.

4. THE PROPOSED FIX IS NOT FREE AS STATED. The claim that the walk's children map "could be shared with cascade" is subtly wrong: the walk's map is built over `surviving` only (resolve.ts:292-299), and SF-1 fork detection is `kids.length > 1`. A shared map built over `linkable` would feed cascaded-away patches into `kids`, manufacturing false forks — an observable behavior change. Fixing that reintroduces a per-entry membership filter or a cleanup pass, recovering much of the cost "saved". The standalone BFS is correct (transitive closure is unique) but is not simpler than the spec transcription.

Remaining true core: with no §5.4 ceiling on chain length (confirmed — ApplyOptions bounds hunks/work/bytes per application only), a self-hostile or key-compromised root author could make cascade quadratic-in-depth. That is a factually accurate but out-of-scope micro-optimization whose fix the project's own audit culture has already declined as over-engineering.

The finding's complexity arithmetic is factually correct — cascade() (resolve.ts:205-216) is a fixpoint loop rescanning all candidates per round, O(N·D) worst case, and §5.4 ceilings (RL-2/RL-3, patch.ts) bound patch application, not chain length. But the finding fails on three counts. (1) Documented deliberate decision: RESOLVE.md §2 (the governing mini-spec required by the Phase 4 gate) explicitly selects this construction — 'Computed as a fixed point over the parent→children relation, which is order-independent by construction' — and RESOLVE.md's confluence table deliberately cites 'the cascade is a fixed point' as the defense against non-commutative folds; ADMIT.md:188-190 characterizes the iteration as intentional. This is reasoned design, not an oversight. (2) Threat model unreachable by third parties: cascade receives `linkable`, which is patches filtered by PT-5 (pubkey === root.pubkey) and PT-6, so only the root author's own key can place candidates into the cascade or add depth; the 'adversarial corpus of ~10k chained patches' requires the victim to sign 10k patches against their own document — self-inflicted, not a DoS vector. (3) Severity overstated and fix not better: by the finding's own citation (AUDIT-2026-07-31 §4: realistic depth ≤1), the loop exits in ≤2 passes and is effectively O(N) on every realistic corpus; the worst case is a ~1s one-time cost on a pathological self-authored input in a pure sans-IO function. The proposed children-map BFS is more machinery than the current 13-line least-fixpoint, churns DEL-2/CHN-2 (explicitly the highest-consequence correctness rules per RESOLVE.md) for zero observable behavior change, and the 'share the walk's children map' point doesn't map cleanly since the walk's map is over `surviving` while cascade would need one over `linkable`. No hard invariant is at stake either way, but an accurate complexity note against a documented deliberate design, with an attacker-unreachable threat model and nil realistic payoff, does not survive as an actionable simplification finding.

The complexity observation is literally accurate (resolve.ts:205-216 rescans `linkable` once per fixpoint round), but the finding fails as a simplification on four grounds.

1. Its central premise is factually wrong. It claims 'no §5.4 ceiling bounds chain length.' §5 4's own table names exactly that: 'Patches per canonical chain ≤ 1000 — Chain-resolution cost' (docs/SPEC-AMENDMENT-BRIEF.md:196-197), carried in v0.6.1 as consumer-side rules RL-2/RL-3 (bounds on total application work, aborted-under-ceiling disposition), RL-5 (a chain stopped by a ceiling is *aborted*, distinct from resolved/HALT), and OV-9 (ceiling outcomes explicitly permit divergence between clients), all implemented in resolve.ts (`aborted` ChainState variant, 'resource-limit' annotations, ApplyOptions passthrough) and enforced on the producer by build.ts RL-1. Chain-resolution cost is a first-class §5.4 resource limit, precisely the answer to the adversarial-corpus scenario the finding invents.

2. The tradeoff is a documented, deliberate design decision. The Phase 3 mini-spec (docs/RESOLVE.md §2 'The kind 5 cascade') prescribes 'Three filters, in this order, then a fixed point' and explains the choice: the transitive closure is order-independent by construction, which matters because UR-1/§7.6 make confluence the load-bearing property of this module. The project's discipline is that algorithmic choices in resolve go through the mini-spec, not an ad-hoc rewrite.

3. The project's measured corpus and cost philosophy make the 'fix' unwarranted complexity. AUDIT-2026-07-31 §4 measured real chain depth at 0-1 (fixpoint = 2 passes, O(N)) and used exactly this evidence to strike D28's byte-bounded LRU as over-engineering ('strike the LRU from D28 rather than implementing it'). DECISIONS-2026-07-27's audit amendments reaffirm not building machinery 'unwarranted by this corpus.' The proposed children-index BFS is the same shape of speculative index the audit already rejected once. Moreover, resolve results are memoized in store.ts behind chainEpoch invalidation (D24), so cascade cost is paid once per topology-invalidating event, not per lookup.

4. The severity math is overstated. Its worst case requires a 10k-deep chain of root-author patches — over §5.4's recommended 1000-patch ceiling, which a conforming consumer aborts under RL-3/RL-5. Even ignoring ceilings, the same adversarial corpus forces the walk to apply 10k unbounded untrusted patches through applyPatchContent; diff application dominates 10^8 hash-set lookups (tens of ms) by orders of magnitude, so the cascade is the least expensive adversarial surface in the function. The equivalence claim in the fix (monotone operator, unique fixpoint, `removed` only membership-tested) is correct -- the proposal is sound, just unneeded and against documented practice.
